questions.stem: This hormone is only produced normally in the body when a woman is pregnant:
questions.why: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is produced by the placenta shortly after implantation.

notes.A: Oestrogen is produced in every menstrual cycle.
notes.C: Progesterone is produced after every ovulation.
notes.D: FSH is secreted throughout reproductive life.
notes.E: LH is secreted throughout reproductive life.

questions.stem: Contractions of the uterus are stimulated by the release of:
questions.why: Oxytocin binds receptors on uterine smooth muscle and increases intracellular calcium, stimulating contractions. Near term, the uterus expresses more oxytocin receptors and becomes more responsive to this signal.

notes.B: FSH promotes ovarian follicle development. Its principal action is not acute contraction of uterine smooth muscle.
notes.C: LH triggers ovulation and supports the corpus luteum. It is not the direct uterotonic signal in labour.
notes.D: Prolactin supports mammary milk production. Uterine contraction is a characteristic action of oxytocin.
notes.E: Oestrogen can increase myometrial responsiveness and oxytocin receptor expression near term. Oxytocin directly stimulates the contraction reflex.

questions.stem: Androgen binding protein is produced by:
questions.why: Sertoli cells produce androgen-binding protein in the seminiferous tubules, especially under FSH stimulation. It helps maintain a high local androgen concentration required for normal spermatogenesis.

notes.A: The adrenal cortex produces adrenal androgens. It is not the source of the Sertoli-cell binding protein in seminiferous tubules.
notes.B: The hypothalamus releases GnRH to regulate pituitary gonadotropins. It does not supply androgen-binding protein to the tubule lumen.
notes.D: Leydig cells make testosterone in response to LH. Sertoli cells supply the binding protein within the seminiferous environment.
notes.E: Ovarian cells produce reproductive steroids, but the testicular androgen-binding protein in this question comes from Sertoli cells.

questions.stem: Early detection of pregnancy depends on detection of:
questions.why: Early pregnancy tests measure hCG in blood or urine. Trophoblast starts producing hCG around implantation, and the hormone helps maintain the corpus luteum and progesterone secretion early in gestation.

notes.A: FSH regulates follicle development and is present in nonpregnant cycles. It is not the marker used for a pregnancy test.
notes.B: Progesterone supports the endometrium and also rises after ovulation in nonpregnant cycles, so it is less specific for early detection.
notes.C: LH surges before ovulation and is structurally related to hCG. Pregnancy assays are designed to detect hCG rather than LH.
notes.E: Oestrogen varies during ordinary menstrual cycles and is not the distinctive early trophoblast marker.

questions.stem: In the normal menstrual cycle:

options.label: A
options.text: the proliferative phase depends on oestrogen secretion

options.label: B
options.text: cervical mucus becomes more fluid around the time of ovulation

options.label: C
options.text: ovulation is observed after a surge in blood luteinizing hormone level

options.label: D
options.text: basal body temperature is higher after ovulation

questions.why: Oestradiol from developing follicles promotes endometrial proliferation and makes cervical mucus more fluid before ovulation. The LH surge triggers ovulation. Progesterone from the corpus luteum then raises basal body temperature slightly.

notes.A: Oestradiol stimulates growth of the endometrium during the proliferative phase.
notes.B: The relatively high oestradiol around ovulation increases the water content of cervical mucus and facilitates sperm passage.
notes.C: The mid-cycle LH surge triggers the events that culminate in release of the oocyte.
notes.D: Progesterone has a thermogenic effect, so basal body temperature rises slightly during the luteal phase.

questions.stem: Fertilization of the human ovum normally:

options.label: B
options.text: prevents further spermatozoa from entering the ovum

options.label: D
options.text: leads to the secretion of human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG) within two weeks

questions.why: Fertilisation usually occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube. Entry of the first sperm triggers changes that limit polyspermy. The developing embryo typically begins implantation about a week later, and trophoblastic hCG becomes detectable during the following days.

notes.A: The ampulla of the uterine tube is the usual site where sperm and oocyte meet.
notes.B: Fusion triggers cortical granule release and changes in the zona pellucida, which help block further sperm entry.
notes.C: Cleavage and transport through the tube take several days. Implantation occurs about six to seven days after fertilisation.
notes.D: Trophoblast produces hCG as implantation begins, and sensitive assays can detect it within roughly two weeks of fertilisation.

questions.stem: Secretion of testosterone:

options.label: B
options.text: causes the epiphyses of long bones to unite

options.label: C
options.text: may lead to a positive nitrogen balance

questions.why: Testosterone participates in negative feedback on LH, promotes protein anabolism and stimulates androgen-dependent body hair. Conversion of testosterone to oestradiol makes an important contribution to growth plate closure at the end of puberty.

notes.A: Testosterone and its aromatised product oestradiol provide feedback to the hypothalamic–pituitary axis, reducing LH drive when androgen levels are sufficient.
notes.B: Oestradiol derived from testosterone promotes fusion of the growth plates in long bones during late puberty.
notes.C: Androgen action favours protein synthesis and can produce positive nitrogen balance, especially during growth.
notes.D: Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone increase terminal hair growth in androgen-sensitive areas of the body.

questions.stem: Human chorionic gonadotrophic hormone (hCG):

options.label: B
options.text: acts directly on the uterus to maintain the endometrium

options.label: C
options.text: is formed in the anterior pituitary

options.label: D
options.text: rises its blood level steadily throughout pregnancy

options.label: E
options.text: can be detected in the urine as an early sign of pregnancy

questions.why: hCG is a glycoprotein hormone produced by the placenta. Its presence in urine is the basis for early pregnancy tests.

notes.A: hCG is a glycoprotein.
notes.B: It acts on the corpus luteum, not directly on the uterus.
notes.C: It is made by the placenta (syncytiotrophoblast).
notes.D: It peaks at 8–10 weeks, then falls.

questions.stem: Compared with the adult, the newborn has less ability to:
questions.why: Several systems continue to mature after birth. Newborns have less efficient bilirubin clearance and renal water handling, less reserve for temperature control, and less mature antibody responses than adults.

notes.A: Hepatic bilirubin uptake and conjugation are less efficient after birth, helping explain the common rise in unconjugated bilirubin.
notes.B: A relatively large surface area and limited cold-defence reserve make temperature harder to maintain, even with brown fat thermogenesis.
notes.C: Newborns can make antibodies, but some responses are less mature. Placental transfer of maternal IgG provides early passive protection.
notes.D: Immature renal filtration and tubular function limit the ability to handle water loads and produce maximally concentrated urine.

questions.stem: Androgens are secreted in the:

options.label: A
options.text: fetus in greater quantities than in early childhood

options.label: D
options.text: male in decreasing quantities after the age of 30

questions.why: Androgens are produced in both sexes. The fetal testis is active during male development and androgen output is low through much of childhood. Ovaries and adrenal cortices contribute to circulating androgens, and average testosterone in men tends to decline with age.

notes.A: Male fetal testosterone rises during genital development. Testicular androgen output is much lower during most of the prepubertal interval.
notes.B: Ovarian theca cells produce androgens, some of which are converted to oestrogens by granulosa cells.
notes.C: The adrenal zona reticularis produces androgens such as DHEA in males as well as in females.
notes.D: Average testosterone can decline after early adulthood. The rate and timing vary considerably between men.

questions.stem: Cryptorchidism means:
questions.why: Cryptorchidism means that one or both testes have not descended into the scrotum. An undescended testis may be located along the normal path of descent, for example in the inguinal canal.

notes.A: Normal descent brings the testes into the scrotum. Cryptorchidism describes a failure of that process.
notes.B: Hypogonadism means deficient gonadal hormone action or function. It is not the anatomical definition of an undescended testis.
notes.C: Excess testicular function does not describe the position of the testes. Cryptorchidism is defined by failure of descent.
notes.E: Priapism is a prolonged penile erection and is unrelated to the testicular position described here.

questions.stem: Fetal haemoglobin:

options.label: A
options.text: is the only type identifiable in fetal blood

options.label: B
options.text: forms the bulk of total haemoglobin for the first year of life

options.label: C
options.text: has a higher oxygen-carrying capacity than adult haemoglobin

options.label: D
options.text: binds 2.3- DPG more avidly than does adult haemoglobin

options.label: E
options.text: has a higher affinity than the adult form for oxygen at low pO2

questions.why: Fetal haemoglobin binds 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate less strongly than adult haemoglobin. Its oxygen dissociation curve is shifted left, helping fetal blood load oxygen from maternal blood at the placenta.

notes.A: Fetal blood contains predominantly haemoglobin F, but other haemoglobin types can be present, including some adult haemoglobin later in gestation.
notes.B: Haemoglobin F decreases after birth as haemoglobin A production rises. It does not normally remain the majority throughout the first year.
notes.C: Haemoglobin F has higher oxygen affinity. Each fully saturated tetramer still carries up to four oxygen molecules, as does adult haemoglobin.
notes.D: Fetal gamma chains reduce binding of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, which contributes to higher oxygen affinity.

questions.stem: For normal development and fertility of spermatozoa there must be:
questions.why: Normal spermatogenesis is supported by high intratesticular testosterone, LH stimulation of Leydig cells and FSH action on Sertoli cells. The scrotum helps maintain a testicular temperature below core temperature, which favours germ cell development.

notes.A: Testosterone supports meiotic and postmeiotic germ cell development and is normally present at high concentrations within the testis.
notes.B: LH activates Leydig cells and promotes testosterone synthesis, supporting the intratesticular androgen supply.
notes.C: FSH acts on Sertoli cells, helping them support germ cell development and normal sperm output.
notes.D: Testicular temperature is normally a few degrees below core temperature. Sustained heating can impair sperm production.

questions.stem: In the mammary glands:

options.label: A
options.text: milk formation can be depressed by hypothalamic activity

options.label: B
options.text: maintenance of lactation depends on suckling

options.label: C
options.text: lactation ceases if the anterior pituitary gland is destroyed

options.label: D
options.text: milk ejection ceases if the posterior pituitary gland is destroyed

questions.why: Milk production depends on prolactin from the anterior pituitary and on regular milk removal. Suckling promotes prolactin release and triggers oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary, which contracts mammary myoepithelial cells for milk ejection.

notes.A: Hypothalamic dopamine inhibits prolactin release from lactotrophs and can therefore suppress milk production.
notes.B: Suckling provides neuroendocrine stimulation as well as repeated milk removal, both important for maintaining supply.
notes.C: Loss of anterior pituitary prolactin removes a key stimulus for milk synthesis and can cause lactation failure.
notes.D: Loss of the usual neurohypophyseal oxytocin release pathway can impair or abolish the normal suckling-triggered milk ejection reflex.

questions.stem: The male postpubertal state differs from the prepubertal in that:

options.label: A
options.text: there is a greater output of 17- ketosteroids in the urine

options.label: B
options.text: skeletal muscle is stronger per unit mass of tissue

options.label: C
options.text: the circulating level of follicle- stimulating hormone (FSH) is higher

options.label: D
options.text: hypothalamic output of gonadotrophin- releasing factors is greater

questions.why: Puberty is marked by increased GnRH, FSH/LH, and androgen production, leading to muscle development and increased urinary 17-ketosteroids.

notes.A: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.B: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.C: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.D: True, but so are the other statements.

questions.stem: The interstitial cells of the testis:

options.label: A
options.text: contribute to the volume of seminal fluid

options.label: B
options.text: are the source of the hormone inhibin

options.label: C
options.text: are stimulated to secrete by luteinizing hormone (LH)

options.label: D
options.text: are stimulated to secrete by FSH

options.label: E
options.text: are non-functional unless the testis descends from the abdomen to the scrotum

questions.why: Testicular interstitial cells are Leydig cells. LH acts on these cells to promote steroidogenesis and testosterone release. FSH primarily acts on adjacent Sertoli cells within the seminiferous tubules.

notes.A: Most seminal fluid volume comes from accessory glands, especially the seminal vesicles and prostate. Leydig cells chiefly secrete testosterone.
notes.B: Inhibin B is produced by Sertoli cells and contributes to feedback on pituitary FSH secretion.
notes.D: FSH acts mainly on Sertoli cells. Leydig steroid production responds primarily to LH.
notes.E: An undescended testis can retain Leydig cell function even when a higher temperature impairs germ cell development and fertility.

questions.stem: Testosterone is secreted by:
questions.why: Leydig cells in testicular interstitial tissue are the main source of testosterone in males. LH stimulates their conversion of cholesterol into steroid hormones.

notes.A: Sertoli cells support spermatogenesis and secrete products such as inhibin B and androgen-binding protein. They are not the principal source of circulating testosterone.
notes.B: The adrenal medulla releases catecholamines. Adrenal androgen precursors come from the cortex.
notes.C: The hypothalamus controls testicular activity indirectly by releasing GnRH, which stimulates pituitary gonadotropins.
notes.E: Pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin. They are not steroid-producing testicular cells.

questions.stem: Ejaculation of semen:

options.label: A
options.text: depends on a spinal cord reflex

options.label: C
options.text: involves rhythmic contractions of striated muscles

options.label: D
options.text: involves contraction of smooth muscle in the vas deferens and seminal vesicles

questions.why: Ejaculation is coordinated by spinal circuits. Sympathetic activity drives emission by contracting smooth muscle in the reproductive ducts and glands. Rhythmic contractions of striated pelvic muscles then help expel semen.

notes.A: Ejaculation is coordinated by spinal reflex circuitry that integrates autonomic and somatic motor output.
notes.B: Sympathetic fibres promote emission of semen into the posterior urethra by activating reproductive tract smooth muscle.
notes.C: Rhythmic contractions of the bulbospongiosus and other perineal muscles help propel semen out of the urethra.
notes.D: Contraction of the vas deferens and seminal vesicles helps move sperm and glandular secretions into the urethra.

questions.stem: Cessation of menstruation (secondary amenorrhoea) may occur because of:

options.label: D
options.text: continuous administration of gonadotropin- releasing hormone (GnRH)

questions.why: Stress and severe energy deficit can suppress hypothalamic GnRH pulses. Continuous exposure to a GnRH agonist can desensitise pituitary receptors, and sustained exogenous sex steroid exposure can suppress normal cycling in some settings. Any of these can lead to amenorrhoea.

notes.A: Psychological stress can disrupt hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility and impair ovulation.
notes.B: Severe weight loss or low energy availability can suppress reproductive signalling and cause functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea.
notes.C: Sustained oestrogen exposure can alter gonadotropin feedback and disrupt ovulatory cycling. Bleeding effects depend on the dose and endometrial exposure.
notes.D: Continuous GnRH receptor stimulation can downregulate pituitary responsiveness. Physiological pulsatile stimulation normally maintains gonadotropin release.

questions.stem: Administration of estrogens and progestogens to women:

options.label: A
options.text: prevents menstruation if given daily throughout the year

options.label: B
options.text: tends to cause salt and water retention

questions.why: Continuous combined oestrogen and progestogen can suppress pituitary gonadotropins and ovulation and can reduce or eliminate scheduled bleeding. Some people still have unscheduled spotting. Oestrogen can also contribute to fluid retention.

notes.A: Continuous use suppresses scheduled withdrawal bleeding by avoiding a hormone-free interval, though complete amenorrhoea is not guaranteed.
notes.B: Oestrogen can affect hepatic angiotensinogen and fluid balance. The degree of salt and water retention varies with the regimen.
notes.C: The hormones provide negative feedback to the hypothalamic–pituitary axis, decreasing normal gonadotropin stimulation.
notes.D: The developing follicle normally requires gonadotropin stimulation and an LH surge for ovulation. The combined hormones can suppress both.

questions.stem: Methods for reducing fertility include:

options.label: A
options.text: bilateral ligation and division of the uterine tubes

options.label: B
options.text: bilateral ligation and division of the vas deferens

options.label: C
options.text: the use of agents which prevent the fertilized ovum from implantation

questions.why: Tubal ligation, vasectomy, IUDs, and barrier methods are all valid fertility control mechanisms.

notes.A: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.B: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.C: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.D: True, but so are the other statements.

questions.stem: Secretion of androgens in the adult female:

options.label: A
options.text: in large amounts can cause enlargement of the clitoris

options.label: C
options.text: may lead to growth of facial hair

questions.why: Sustained severe androgen excess in an adult woman can cause virilisation, including clitoral enlargement, voice deepening and more terminal facial hair. It can also disrupt normal ovarian cycling and cause amenorrhoea.

notes.A: Marked or prolonged androgen excess can stimulate clitoral growth.
notes.B: Androgen effects on the larynx and vocal folds can deepen the voice during virilisation.
notes.C: Androgen-sensitive facial hair follicles can produce more terminal hair, causing hirsutism.
notes.D: Excess androgen can accompany impaired ovulation and lead to irregular cycles or amenorrhoea.
